_notes: Entries from Table 2 of the 2023 AGS Beers Criteria (potentially inappropriate medication use in older adults). Each entry was checked against the published table on the date in its `verifiedOn` field; see docs/DATA_VERIFICATION.md. This is a partial list and the wording is paraphrased. Many entries only apply at certain doses, durations or indications, which this app does not know; the recommendation text states those conditions. Not medical advice.

sources: American Geriatrics Society 2023 updated AGS Beers Criteria for potentially inappropriate medication use in older adults. J Am Geriatr Soc. 2023;71(7):2052-2081. Full text read from PubMed Central (author manuscript): https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12478568/
NLM RxNorm and RxClass (https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/) for brand-name ingredients and for membership of classes the paper names without listing drugs.
verification.rule: Matchers ignore any entry whose `verified` value is not "confirmed" or "corrected".
verification.minimumAgeBasis: The paper states the criteria are intended to be applied to adults 65 years old and older.

source: American Geriatrics Society 2023 updated AGS Beers Criteria for potentially inappropriate medication use in older adults. J Am Geriatr Soc. 2023;71(7):2052-2081.

entries.reason: Strongly anticholinergic. Older adults clear these drugs more slowly, and they can cause confusion, dry mouth, constipation and other anticholinergic effects.
entries.recommendation: Avoid. For diphenhydramine this applies to oral forms. Use of diphenhydramine for the acute treatment of a severe allergic reaction may be appropriate.
entries.verifiedAgainst: Table 2, row "First-generation antihistamines"; brand names checked in RxNorm
entries.verificationNote: Removed the brand alias "advil pm": RxNorm could not resolve it to ingredients in this session. Added the table's "(oral)" qualifier for diphenhydramine to the recommendation.

entries.reason: Older adults are more sensitive to benzodiazepines and break down the long-acting ones more slowly. They raise the risk of cognitive impairment, delirium, falls, fractures and car crashes.
entries.recommendation: Avoid. May be appropriate for seizure disorders, REM sleep behavior disorder, benzodiazepine withdrawal, alcohol withdrawal, severe generalized anxiety disorder, and anesthesia around a procedure.
entries.verifiedAgainst: Table 2, row "Benzodiazepines"; brand names checked in RxNorm
entries.verificationNote: Removed "Do not stop suddenly" from the recommendation: it is not in the table. Completed the list of situations the table says may be appropriate.

entries.reason: Side effects in older adults are similar to benzodiazepines (delirium, falls, fractures, more emergency visits and hospital stays, car crashes), with little improvement in sleep.
entries.recommendation: Avoid.
entries.verifiedAgainst: Table 2, row "Nonbenzodiazepine benzodiazepine receptor agonist hypnotics (Z-drugs)"; brand names checked in RxNorm

entries.reason: Highly anticholinergic and sedating, and can cause a drop in blood pressure on standing.
entries.recommendation: Avoid. For doxepin this applies to doses above 6 mg per day; lower doses have a safety profile similar to placebo.
entries.verifiedAgainst: Table 2, row "Antidepressants with strong anticholinergic activity"; brand names checked in RxNorm
entries.verificationNote: The table lists doxepin only above 6 mg/day. A name cannot show the dose, so the recommendation states the limit.

entries.reason: Poorly tolerated by older adults because of anticholinergic effects, sedation and a higher risk of fractures. Effectiveness at doses older adults can tolerate is questionable.
entries.recommendation: Avoid.
entries.verifiedAgainst: Table 2, row "Skeletal muscle relaxants"; brand names checked in RxNorm

entries.reason: Higher risk of cardiovascular events, death from any cause, and low blood sugar than alternative agents. Long-acting ones (glyburide, glimepiride) carry a higher risk of prolonged low blood sugar.
entries.recommendation: Avoid as first- or second-line monotherapy or add-on therapy unless there are substantial barriers to safer and more effective agents. If one is used, a short-acting agent such as glipizide is preferred over a long-acting one such as glyburide or glimepiride.
entries.verifiedAgainst: Table 2, row "Sulfonylureas (all, including short- and longer-acting)"; brand names checked in RxNorm
entries.verificationNote: Recommendation reworded to match the table: "first- or second-line monotherapy or add-on therapy".

entries.reason: Long-term use is linked to C. difficile infection, pneumonia, gastrointestinal cancers, bone loss and fractures.
entries.recommendation: Avoid scheduled use for more than 8 weeks unless for high-risk patients (such as those taking oral corticosteroids or long-term NSAIDs), erosive esophagitis, Barrett esophagitis, a pathologic hypersecretory condition, or a demonstrated need for maintenance treatment.
entries.verifiedAgainst: Table 2, row "Proton-pump inhibitors"; brand names checked in RxNorm
entries.verificationNote: Added the "pathologic hypersecretory condition" exception, which the recommendation had left out.

entries.reason: Higher risk of stomach or intestinal bleeding and ulcers, especially over age 75 or when taken with corticosteroids, blood thinners or antiplatelet medicines. Can also raise blood pressure and harm the kidneys.
entries.recommendation: Avoid chronic use unless other options are not effective and a stomach-protecting medicine can be taken. Avoid short-term scheduled use together with corticosteroids, anticoagulants or antiplatelet agents unless a stomach-protecting medicine can be taken. Applies to oral use.
entries.verifiedAgainst: Table 2, row "Non-COX-2-selective NSAIDs, oral"; brand names checked in RxNorm
entries.verificationNote: The table row also lists aspirin above 325 mg/day (left out: a name cannot show the dose) and indomethacin and ketorolac (covered by their own entry).

entries.reason: Higher risk of stomach or intestinal bleeding, ulcers and kidney injury in older adults. Of all NSAIDs, indomethacin has the most side effects, including effects on the brain.
entries.recommendation: Avoid. For ketorolac this applies to oral and injected forms.
entries.verifiedAgainst: Table 2, row "Indomethacin / Ketorolac (oral and parenteral)"; brand names checked in RxNorm
entries.verificationNote: Added the table's "oral and parenteral" qualifier for ketorolac to the recommendation.

entries.class: Aspirin for primary prevention of cardiovascular disease
entries.reason: The risk of major bleeding from aspirin rises sharply with age, and studies show no net benefit when it is started for primary prevention in older adults.
entries.recommendation: Avoid starting aspirin for primary prevention of cardiovascular disease, and consider stopping it in older adults already taking it for primary prevention. This does not apply to secondary prevention in people with established cardiovascular disease, where aspirin is generally indicated.
entries.verifiedAgainst: Table 2, row "Aspirin for primary prevention of cardiovascular disease"; brand names checked in RxNorm; "acetylsalicylic acid" resolves to aspirin in RxNorm
entries.verificationNote: Replaced "after a heart attack, stroke or stent" with the table's wording about secondary prevention in established cardiovascular disease.

entries.reason: Compared with direct oral anticoagulants, warfarin has a higher risk of major bleeding, particularly bleeding in the brain, with similar or lower effectiveness for nonvalvular atrial fibrillation and venous thromboembolism.
entries.recommendation: Avoid starting warfarin as initial therapy for nonvalvular atrial fibrillation or venous thromboembolism unless alternatives are contraindicated or there are substantial barriers to their use. For people who have used warfarin long-term, it may be reasonable to continue it, particularly with well-controlled INRs and no adverse effects.
entries.verifiedAgainst: Table 2, row "Warfarin for the treatment of nonvalvular atrial fibrillation or venous thromboembolism"; brand names checked in RxNorm

entries.reason: High rate of physical dependence, tolerance to sleep benefits, and a greater risk of overdose at low doses.
entries.recommendation: Avoid.
entries.verifiedAgainst: Table 2, row "Barbiturates"; brand names checked in RxNorm

entries.reason: Increased risk of stroke, and a greater rate of cognitive decline and death in people with dementia.
entries.recommendation: Avoid, except for FDA-approved indications such as schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, Parkinson disease psychosis, add-on treatment of major depressive disorder, or short-term use for nausea.
entries.verifiedAgainst: Table 2, row "Antipsychotics, first- (typical) and second- (atypical) generation" and footnote d; brand names checked in RxNorm
entries.verificationNote: Ziprasidone is named in footnote d rather than in the row itself.

entries.reason: High risk of a drop in blood pressure on standing and related harms. Other blood pressure medicines have a better balance of risk and benefit.
entries.recommendation: Avoid use as a treatment for high blood pressure.
entries.verifiedAgainst: Table 2, row "Non-selective peripheral alpha-1 blockers for the treatment of hypertension"; brand names checked in RxNorm

entries.reason: High risk of side effects on the brain and nervous system, and may cause a slow heart rate and a drop in blood pressure on standing.
entries.recommendation: Avoid clonidine as a first-line treatment for high blood pressure. Avoid other central alpha-agonists for high blood pressure.
entries.verifiedAgainst: Table 2, row "Central alpha-agonists for the treatment of hypertension"; brand names checked in RxNorm

entries.reason: Safer and more effective options exist for atrial fibrillation and heart failure. Older adults clear digoxin more slowly, and higher doses add risk of toxicity without added benefit.
entries.recommendation: Avoid as first-line therapy for atrial fibrillation or heart failure. If used, avoid doses above 0.125 mg per day.
entries.verifiedAgainst: Table 2, row "Digoxin for first-line treatment of atrial fibrillation or heart failure"; brand names checked in RxNorm

entries.reason: Effective for keeping a normal heart rhythm, but has greater toxicities than other medicines used for atrial fibrillation.
entries.recommendation: Avoid as first-line therapy for atrial fibrillation unless the person has heart failure or substantial thickening of the left ventricle.
entries.verifiedAgainst: Table 2, row "Amiodarone"; brand names checked in RxNorm

entries.reason: Potential for lung and liver toxicity and nerve damage, especially with long-term use.
entries.recommendation: Avoid in people with creatinine clearance below 30 mL/min, and avoid long-term use to suppress infections.
entries.verifiedAgainst: Table 2, row "Nitrofurantoin"; also Table 6, row "Nitrofurantoin"; brand names checked in RxNorm

entries.reason: Highly anticholinergic, with uncertain effectiveness.
entries.recommendation: Avoid.
entries.verifiedAgainst: Table 2, row "GI antispasmodics with strong anticholinergic activity"; brand names checked in RxNorm
entries.verificationNote: The table row also lists atropine (excluding ophthalmic) and clidinium-chlordiazepoxide, which this entry leaves out.

entries.reason: Can cause movement disorders, including tardive dyskinesia. The risk may be greater in frail older adults and with prolonged use.
entries.recommendation: Avoid, unless for gastroparesis, and then generally for no longer than 12 weeks.
entries.verifiedAgainst: Table 2, row "Metoclopramide"; brand names checked in RxNorm

entries.reason: Minimal effect on weight, and increases the risk of blood clots and possibly death in older adults.
entries.recommendation: Avoid.
entries.verifiedAgainst: Table 2, row "Megestrol"; brand names checked in RxNorm

entries.reason: Not an effective oral pain reliever at commonly used doses, and has a higher risk of neurotoxicity, including delirium, than other opioids.
entries.recommendation: Avoid.
entries.verifiedAgainst: Table 2, row "Meperidine"; brand names checked in RxNorm; "pethidine" resolves to meperidine in RxNorm

entries.reason: High risk of low blood sodium. Safer alternatives exist.
entries.recommendation: Avoid for treatment of nighttime urination.
entries.verifiedAgainst: Table 2, row "Desmopressin"; brand names checked in RxNorm
